source_text:
Fragmenta in epistulam ad Titum (in catenis)
Tit 1,12®13a Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ποιητὴς ὁ εἰρηκὼς τὸ Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία,
γαστέρες ἀργαί, ἐπιλαμβανόμενος αὐτῶν εἶπεν ὡς κακῶς δεικνύντων τάφον ∆ιὸς
τὸν οὐκ ὄντα, ἐχρήσατο δὲ τῷ αὐτῷ στίχῳ Παῦλος, ἴνα μὴ νομισθῇ τῷ ποιητῇ
συντρέχειν καὶ τῷ λεγομένῳ ∆ιῒ μαρτυρεῖν ἀθανασίαν, ἐπήγαγεν· ἡ μαρτυρία αὕτη
ἀληθής ἐστιν. ἐκεῖνος ἐψεύσατο τῷ ∆ιῒ συνηγορῶν, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀληθεύω λέγων ὅτι οἱ
Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσταί εἰσιν καὶ γαστέρες ἀργαί. αὕτη ἡ μαρτυρία ἀληθής, οὐκ ἐκείνη.
thought_title: Paul's use of the poet's line about Cretans
orientation: Oecumenius opens by explaining why Paul, after quoting the pagan poet's line about Cretans, added that this testimony is true.
pass_a_gloss: Since the poet who said 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons,' seizing on them, said that they wrongly point to a tomb of Zeus that does not exist, and Paul used the same verse, so that he might not be thought to run together with the poet and to testify immortality to the so-called Zeus, he added: 'This testimony is true.' That one lied, speaking in defense of Zeus, but I speak truth, saying that the Cretans are always liars and idle gluttons. This testimony is true, not that one.

lemmas.gloss: to run together with, agree with

choices.why: The participle has an adversative force: the poet attacked the Cretans for their claim about Zeus's tomb.
The adverb κακῶς modifies the participle: the Cretans were wrong to point to a tomb of Zeus.
The phrase modifies τάφον: the tomb is non-existent because Zeus is immortal.
The verb suggests agreement or alignment; Paul wanted to avoid appearing to side with the poet.
The participle λεγομένῳ distances Paul from the pagan god; Oecumenius signals that Zeus is only 'so-called.'
The demonstrative contrasts the poet with Paul's 'I' in the next clause.

bible_refs.note: Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί

pass_b_english: The poet who said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons,” was attacking them for wrongly pointing to a tomb of Zeus that does not exist. Paul used that same line, but so that he would not be thought to agree with the poet and testify to the immortality of the so-called Zeus, he added: “This testimony is true” (Titus 1:13). Paul means: That poet lied when he spoke in defense of Zeus, but Paul speaks the truth when he says that Cretans are always liars and idle gluttons. This testimony is true, not that one.

The speaker issue about 'That poet lied... but I speak the truth' is real and has been fixed by clarifying that Paul is the speaker.
